messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 67
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Military Medic
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 64

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident, Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Thought Monitoring: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy, Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
  Memory: Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person

Vignette:
Arthur Vance was pulling out of the veterans’ medical center parking lot when a semi tractor-trailer mounted the curb and struck his sedan broadside. The impact threw him forward, seatbelt locking hard against his collarbone. He lay pinned in the twisting wreckage for nearly four minutes before a firefighter pried the door open. As he crawled onto the asphalt, the smell of ruptured gasoline and burning rubber filled the air, sharp and suffocating. He tried to assess the driver of the truck, a man slumped over the wheel, but his hands trembled uncontrollably. He knew his training as a military medic meant he should have been steady, should have followed protocol. Instead, he had hesitated, had fumbled his kit, had let the man’s eyes go still before he could even check a pulse. He had come to believe the event happened because of the way he acted, that if he had moved faster, acted with the precision expected of him, the man would still be breathing. In the weeks that followed, Arthur’s body refused to quiet down. Ordinary noises—a fork clattering on a plate, a car door shutting three streets over, the sudden ring of his home telephone—made him jolt upright, heart hammering against his ribs as if bracing for another impact. He found himself constantly monitoring his own thoughts, watching for any sign that his mind was slipping, that he was losing control or going mad. He fought hard to push the images of the twisted metal and the driver’s face out of his head, forcing his attention onto crossword puzzles or the evening news. But the memories returned not as a coherent story but as disjointed fragments. When he tried to explain the accident to his grandson, he would start detailing the skid, then lose the thread, his voice trailing off as a sudden ringing echoed in his mind, layered with the wet crunch of glass and the groan of metal. The experience no longer felt like his own; it sat inside him like a foreign object, detached and unanchored. The habit of avoidance settled over his months like a heavy blanket. Arthur stopped driving altogether. He could not tolerate being behind the wheel, and riding as a passenger in a car made his chest tighten with a familiar, suffocating dread. At the veterans’ clinic where he still processed cases, the sight of a maintenance crew loading a dolly with industrial solvent triggered a sudden wave of nausea. He began routing his breaks to the far stairwell, avoiding the main corridors where the hum of machinery or the sudden impact of a closing door made his shoulders lock. He could no longer trust that he would do the right thing under pressure, and he viewed his own need for protection as a fundamental flaw. He was a weak person, he decided, someone who had failed the very standards he had spent decades teaching others to uphold. He gradually transferred to a desking role, processing paperwork from a corner cubicle where he could control the door and the noise. His retirement from clinical duties left him isolated in the quiet of his bungalow. He rarely invited anyone over, mostly because the sharp tang of a neighbor’s open bottle of grain alcohol or the acrid smell of a misfiring furnace vent triggered a violent flash of the crash scene. When his neighbor mowed his lawn late on a Saturday, the heavy scent of exhaust and heated rubber made Arthur drop his coffee cup and press his palms flat against the kitchen counter, breathing in short, measured gasps until the tremor in his hands passed. He had stopped attending his late wife’s family gatherings, telling himself he was too busy, when the truth was he could not bear the confined space of the church hall or the sudden clatter of serving trays. What frightened him most was the certainty that another accident was inevitable, that his own body would betray him at the worst possible moment. After years of walking through his days with a coiled spring in his chest, Arthur finally sat down with the clinic’s intake coordinator. He was not sure if his mind could ever be trusted again, but he was hoping that someone might show him how to live without constantly bracing for the next impact.
